rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not exhaust himself trying to guide people: his task is to convey the message, while God alone grants guidance and knows who merits it.
rows.anchor: His responsibility is to communicate the message to them. He does not have the authority or power to make them accept guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh feared that accepting Islam would unite Arabia against them and drive them out; they saw polytheism, tribal idols at the Kaaba, and their religious leadership as the basis of their political dominance.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh thought that it was because of thei r religion of polytheism that they have political authority in Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi compares the Quraysh’s fear of losing their order with modern leaders’ objections to Islamic systems and with Pharaoh’s courtiers’ charge against Moses, cited at 20:63.
rows.anchor: precisely the same objection was raised by the courtiers and l eaders of the Pharaoh against the teachings of Moses (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answers that when Abraham settled his descendants in Mecca, the place lacked both security and economic resources, yet he settled them there and prayed for their provision and safety.
rows.anchor: neither were the lives of people secure, nor did there exist any economic resources to live there. Yet Abraham (sws) did so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mecca’s produce and seasonal blessings came through God’s grace and Abraham’s prayer; Quraysh wrongly feared ruin from the Abrahamic religion that had brought them these benefits.
rows.anchor: all these blessings that they enjoyed awere the result of God’s grace and Abraham’s prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words lament that most Quraysh do not know their own history.
rows.anchor: express sorrow on the attitude of these people: their majority is not aware of their own history.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects the protected sanctuary and Quraysh’s ingratitude to 29:67, which contrasts Mecca’s safety with the insecurity around it.
rows.anchor: In S ūrah al-‘Ankab ūt, this topic is brought up thus:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ثمرات includes food-related produce of many kinds, not only fruits.
rows.anchor: it does not merely refer to fruits.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction meaning God established the sanctuary for them parallels the construction in 24:55.
rows.anchor: The construction ﻧﻤَﻜ	ﻦۡ ﻟ	َﻬﻢۡ is similar to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the House a secure sanctuary that does not depend on others for protection and in fact protects others; Sūrah Quraysh will discuss this further.
rows.anchor: This is a fact and history bears witness to it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: بطر means acting arrogantly and haughtily; in this verse it also conveys ingratitude toward a favor by treating it as trivial.
rows.anchor: he showed ingratitude to a favour by regarding it to be trivial

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentators explain the accusative معيشتها through an omitted genitive particle or locative; Islahi rejects those analyses and instead understands بطر as conveying ingratitude by trivializing a favor.
rows.anchor: he showed ingratitude to a favour by regarding it to be trivial

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farāhī treats معيشتها as the direct object of أهلكنا; Islahi rejects that analysis and reads بطر as conveying ingratitude by trivializing a favor.
rows.anchor: he showed ingratitude to a favour by regarding it to be trivial

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpreters explain the transitive use through taḍmīn, with بطر carrying an added sense of treating a favor as insignificant; Islahi finds this account acceptable.
rows.anchor: a verb encompassing the meaning of another verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh attributed Mecca’s peace and prosperity to their own strategy, though these were God’s favors that called for gratitude rather than pride.
rows.anchor: They thought that the peace and prosperity this land enjoyed was as a result of their planning and hence they were very proud of their strategy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier nations were destroyed for arrogance over their favors, and Quraysh regularly passed the remains of such nations on their trade routes.
rows.anchor: God destroyed them because of this attitude

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative تلک indicates familiar settlements, including the lands of Thamūd and Lot, which Quraysh encountered along their trade routes.
rows.anchor: shows that these settlements were known to the addressees.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of settlements no longer inhabited except briefly corresponds to the account in Hūd 11:100.
rows.anchor: This is an account of these settlements that We narrate to you. Some of them are intact and others do not exist

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording can also mean that the settlements lost their former grandeur, even if shepherds or nomads sometimes inhabited them.
rows.anchor: it may be that at times some shepherds and nomads may have inhabited them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God the inheritor means that the places and possessions of former rulers returned to their true owner, who owns the heavens and earth.
rows.anchor: all those who regarded themselves to be the owners and rulers of these places and what they owned came into the ownership of God because it is He Who is the real owner of the heavens and the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s established practice is not to destroy a city before sending a messenger to its central city to recite revelations; its people are punished only after they become unjust.
rows.anchor: The verse states that regarding decisive worldly punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Quraysh, the first stage of this practice was complete: God had sent a messenger to Mecca, so their response to his continual warnings would determine what followed.
rows.anchor: God had sent His messenger to Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about God not destroying cities introduces a second phase of the divine practice described in the passage.
rows.anchor: mention the second phase of this divine practice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who mislead others bear their own sins and responsibility for leading others astray; they cannot transfer that burden to their followers, as also stated at 39:7.
rows.anchor: they will be bearing the burden of their sins and will also bear the responsibility of leading others astray.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elders’ assurance that they would carry the younger people’s burdens is mistaken: they will answer for their own sins and for leading others astray.
rows.anchor: the elders who are reassuring their young ones that they will bear their burdens are under a grave misconception and wrongly assuring the younger ones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The referenced words concern self-invented religious practices falsely attributed to God; those who force others to adopt them remain accountable for these sins.
rows.anchor: religious innovations which they invented themselves but ascribed them to God. Such is their extremism that they compel others to adopt them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding passage teaches that those who serve God’s cause must undergo trials, through which their sincerity and truthfulness are tested.
rows.anchor: those who take up the cause of God do not reach their destination without any hindrance or barriers. They have to pass through many trials

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding passage affirms individual accountability before God; social or material coercion does not excuse a person’s religious deviation.
rows.anchor: in matters of religion, each person is accountable himself before God. No other person will bear his burden.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who oppress truth-seekers to turn them from religion are granted respite, but increasing rebellion brings God’s inescapable judgment.
rows.anchor: people who subject those who tread the path of truth to various oppressions in order to turn them away from religion are given respite from God till a certain time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The following verses develop these themes through accounts of God’s prophets and the people who opposed and rejected them.
rows.anchor: In the succeeding verses, the facts stated above are delineated through the accounts of the prophets of God and their enemies and rejecters.
